drills.title: Toe Taps
drills.how: Alternate feet tapping the top of the ball quickly.
coachingPoints: Coordination, rhythm
Alternate feet tapping the top of the ball quickly.
Quality over speed — make every rep count.
instructions: Place the ball on the ground in front of you on a flat surface.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent.
Tap the top of the ball lightly with the sole of your right foot, then immediately switch to your left foot.
Keep alternating feet in a quick rhythm — right, left, right, left.
Stay on the balls of your feet the entire time. Do not let your heels touch the ground.
Keep your eyes up after the first few reps — do not stare at the ball.
Complete the full set without losing the ball. If the ball rolls away, reset and continue.

drills.title: Inside Touches
drills.how: Pass the ball between feet using only the inside.
coachingPoints: Soft touch
Pass the ball between feet using only the inside.
Quality over speed — make every rep count.
instructions: Place the ball in front of you. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Roll the ball sideways using the sole of your right foot, from right to left.
Stop the ball with the inside of your left foot.
Now roll the ball back from left to right using the sole of your left foot.
Stop the ball with the inside of your right foot.
Repeat the rolling motion, alternating feet, building a smooth rhythm.
Keep your body low and balanced throughout. Use small, controlled rolls.

drills.title: Sole Rolls
drills.how: Roll ball across body using the sole, alternating feet.
coachingPoints: Sole control
Roll ball across body using the sole, alternating feet.
Quality over speed — make every rep count.
instructions: Place the ball in front of you. Stand with your right foot on top of the ball.
Pull the ball back toward you using the sole of your right foot.
As the ball reaches your standing foot, push it diagonally forward with the inside of your right foot, forming a V shape.
Let the ball roll forward into space, then step to it and repeat with the same foot.
After completing reps on the right foot, switch to the left foot.
Focus on smooth transitions — the pull-back and push-forward should feel like one connected movement.
Keep your head up and your body balanced over the ball.

disciplines.name: Psychological
disciplines.tagline: Train the mind like a muscle.
disciplines.blurb: Guided mental exercises built for soccer: self-talk, focus, confidence, composure, and match mentality. Short, practical, and designed to pair with your on-pitch training.

categories.name: Self-Talk
categories.focus: What you say to yourself between touches decides your next touch.

levels.name: Foundation
levels.theme: Notice the voice, then choose the words.

drills.title: Catch and Flip
drills.how: Learn to catch a negative thought mid-session and flip it into an instruction.
coachingPoints: A flipped thought is an instruction, not a wish
Short phrases beat long speeches
Catching the thought is the win — flipping gets easier
steps: Think back to your last training session or match. Find one moment where your inner voice turned negative — after a bad touch, a missed shot, a lost duel.
Write the exact thought down in your head, word for word. Example: 'I always lose the ball under pressure.'
Now flip it into an instruction for your body: 'Big first touch away from pressure.' Negative thoughts describe the past — instructions aim at the next action.
Create your flip pairs: pick your three most common negative thoughts and build one short instruction for each.
In your next session, your only mental job is to catch one negative thought live and say the flip — out loud if you're alone.
drills.journalPrompt: What is your most common negative thought on the pitch, and what instruction will replace it?

drills.title: Your Power Phrase
drills.how: Build one short phrase that describes the player you are becoming, and attach it to your training.
coachingPoints: Present tense — 'I am', never 'I will be'
Five words or fewer
It should feel slightly bold — that's the point
steps: Describe, in one sentence, the player you want to be in twelve months. Be specific: what do teammates and coaches see?
Cut that sentence down to five words or fewer, in the present tense. Examples: 'I demand the ball.' 'My first touch is calm.' 'I press first.'
Say it to yourself three times slowly. If it feels flat, sharpen it until it creates a small spark.
Attach it to a trigger: say your phrase every time you tie your boots, and once more as you step onto the pitch.
Use it for two weeks before changing it. Repetition is what turns a phrase into identity.
drills.journalPrompt: Write your power phrase. Why does this one fit the player you're becoming?

drills.title: The Reset Word
drills.how: Install a one-word reset that ends a mistake the moment it happens.
coachingPoints: The mistake is over the moment the word is said
Pair the word with a physical action
Elite players have the shortest memories on the pitch
steps: Recall how long a mistake usually stays in your head during a match. One pass? One minute? One half?
Choose a one-word reset. Common choices: 'Next.' 'Now.' 'Go.' Pick the one that feels natural in your voice.
Pair it with a physical action — clap your hands once, touch the grass, pull your socks up. The body action anchors the word.
Rehearse it: imagine giving the ball away cheaply. Feel the flash of frustration. Say your word, do your action, and picture yourself sprinting into position.
Repeat that rehearsal three times with three different mistakes: a missed shot, a bad touch, a failed tackle.
Rule for your next session: every mistake gets the word and the action within two seconds. Track how many you catch.
drills.journalPrompt: What's your reset word and action? What mistake is hardest for you to let go of?

levels.name: Match Application
levels.theme: Take the words into the game.

drills.title: First-Five Script
drills.how: Script what you say to yourself in the first five minutes of a match, when nerves are loudest.
coachingPoints: Early simple actions silence nerves faster than any thought
Your script tells you what to DO, not how to feel
Same script every match — familiarity kills anxiety
steps: Recall how you usually feel in the first five minutes of a match. Racing heart? Hiding from the ball? Forcing things?
Decide your first three simple actions: e.g. 'First touch: one-touch pass backwards. First duel: win the body contact. First sprint: full speed, even off the ball.'
Turn them into a three-line script you can say in the tunnel or on the kickoff line. Keep each line under six words.
Rehearse the script now: close your eyes, hear the whistle, and walk through your first three actions in real time.
After your next match, score yourself: did you complete your three actions inside five minutes?
drills.journalPrompt: Write your three first-five actions. Which one calms you down fastest?

drills.title: Talk Like a Captain
drills.how: Train your outward voice — what you say to teammates shapes what you believe about yourself.
coachingPoints: Information beats noise — tell teammates what they can use
Encourage within five seconds of a teammate's mistake
A talking player is never out of the game
steps: Count honestly: in your last match, how many times did you communicate something useful — 'man on', 'turn', 'time', a name before a pass?
Set your talk targets for the next session: ten useful calls per half, and one encouragement within five seconds whenever a teammate makes a mistake.
Rehearse the calls out loud now so they're automatic: 'Man on. Turn. Time. Switch it. Well in. Again, again.'
Notice the side effect: when you talk, you scan more, you stay in the game after your own mistakes, and your body language stays tall.
After the session, count your calls. Below target means your focus drifted inward — that's the signal to talk more, not less.
drills.journalPrompt: Which call do you make the least? What stops you from using your voice?

drills.title: Post-Match Voice Review
drills.how: Review the voice in your head after a match the same way you'd review your touches.
coachingPoints: Review the voice, not just the performance
One harsh thought rewritten is real training
Do this within 24 hours of the match
steps: Think back over your most recent match or hard session.
Find the loudest negative thing your inner voice said. Where in the game was it? What triggered it?
Find one moment your inner voice helped you — a reset, an instruction, a spark of confidence.
Rewrite the negative line the way a great coach would say it: honest about the mistake, pointed at the fix.
Answer the journal question below to log your review.
drills.journalPrompt: What did your inner voice say at your worst moment, and what's the coach's version of that line?

categories.name: Focus
categories.focus: Attention is a skill. Train where your eyes and mind go.

levels.name: Foundation
levels.theme: Hold attention on one thing, bring it back when it drifts.

drills.title: One-Ball Focus Block
drills.how: A ten-minute training block where your only job is total attention on the ball.
coachingPoints: Drifting is normal — returning is the skill
Phone out of sight, not just on silent
Quality of attention beats quantity of reps
steps: Set up any simple ball mastery drill you know well — toe taps, sole rolls, inside-outside touches.
Remove every distraction: phone away, no music with lyrics, face away from anything moving.
Train for ten minutes with one rule: full attention on the ball and your feet. Feel each touch.
Each time your mind drifts — and it will — silently count the drift ('one... two...') and bring attention back to the ball without frustration.
At the end, remember your drift count. The count going down across sessions is focus getting stronger.
drills.journalPrompt: How many times did your mind drift, and where did it go?

drills.title: Box Breathing
drills.how: A four-count breathing pattern that steadies the mind and becomes your pre-action anchor.
coachingPoints: In through the nose, out through the mouth
Shoulders stay down and loose
This same breath works seconds before a penalty
steps: Sit or stand tall. You'll breathe in a square: in for 4 seconds, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4.
Complete 6 full cycles with the animation. Eyes on the circle, attention on the air moving.
Notice the change: heart rate down, shoulders lower, mind quieter. This state is available to you any time — on the bench, before kickoff, at a penalty.
Finish with one normal breath and your power phrase from Self-Talk.
drills.journalPrompt: Where in a match would this breath help you most?

drills.title: Scan Counting
drills.how: Build the habit of lifting your eyes off the ball on a rhythm — the foundation of awareness.
coachingPoints: Scan BEFORE the ball arrives, not after
A scan is a question: where is space, who is close?
Eyes up is a habit, and habits are built on rhythm
steps: Set up a simple two-touch wall pass or passing drill against a wall or with a partner.
Rule: between your touches, lift your eyes and look over one shoulder. Ball travels — you scan. Ball arrives — eyes back.
Make each scan a real question. First block: where is the most space? Second block: where would a defender be?
Count your scans for two minutes. Rest. Then beat your count without rushing your touch.
Finish by noticing: did your touch get worse when you scanned? With reps, it won't — that's the skill.
drills.journalPrompt: What did you actually SEE when you scanned, and what surprised you?

levels.name: Match Application
levels.theme: Refocus fast inside the chaos of a game.

drills.title: Trigger-Word Refocus
drills.how: Choose a trigger word that snaps your attention back to the game when it drifts.
coachingPoints: Drift isn't failure — slow return is the only failure
Attach the word to your next physical action
One word, said sharply, beats a lecture to yourself
steps: List your three most common in-game distractions: the referee's last call, the scoreline, a mistake, someone on the sideline.
Choose a trigger word that means 'back to now' — 'Here.' 'Ball.' 'Sharp.' Different from your mistake-reset word.

Rehearse: imagine you're mid-match, replaying an argument with the referee in your head. Say the trigger word and immediately pick one thing in the game to lock onto — the ball, your runner, the nearest opponent.
Run that rehearsal for each of your three distractions.
Next match rule: every drift gets the trigger word plus one concrete observation about what's happening right now.
drills.journalPrompt: What pulls your attention out of matches most often?

drills.title: Dead-Ball Switch
drills.how: Use dead-ball moments to rest attention, then switch it back on as play restarts.
coachingPoints: Nobody holds maximum focus for 90 minutes — pacing wins
Breath down, eyes up, job named
The switch-on must finish BEFORE the ball moves
steps: Understand the idea: attention is a battery. Goal kicks, throw-ins, injuries, and substitutions are charging moments — if you use them.
Learn the down-shift: at a dead ball, drop your shoulders, take one slow breath out, let your eyes soften for two seconds.
Learn the up-shift: as the restart approaches, name your next job out loud or in your head — 'mark seven', 'drop to cover', 'show for it' — and get your feet alive.
Rehearse the full cycle three times: whistle... down-shift... referee ready... up-shift... play.
Next match, run the cycle at every dead ball in one half and notice your energy in the final ten minutes.
drills.journalPrompt: In which part of a match does your focus usually fade first?

drills.title: Pre-Training Minute
drills.how: One minute before every session: set a single intention so the session has a target.
coachingPoints: One intention per session, never three
Make it observable — you should be able to count it
An aimed session is worth two aimless ones
steps: Before your next session, take sixty seconds alone.
Ask: what is the ONE thing this session is for? Make it small and countable — 'scan before every reception', 'ten calls per half', 'attack the front post twice'.
Say it once as a sentence: 'Today is for ___.'
After the session, give yourself a score out of ten on that one thing only — not on the whole session.
drills.journalPrompt: What is your next session for? One thing only.

categories.name: Confidence
categories.focus: Confidence is built from evidence, not hype.

drills.title: Highlight Replay
drills.how: Replay your three best moments in full detail — the brain strengthens what you rehearse.
coachingPoints: First person — through your own eyes, not a camera
Detail is what makes it work: sounds, grass, contact
Replay the FEELING, not just the footage
steps: Sit somewhere quiet. Close your eyes after reading each step. Choose your three best moments ever on a pitch — a goal, a tackle, a pass, a save, a full match.
Replay moment one through your own eyes. See the pitch, hear the sounds, feel the contact with the ball. Slow it down at the best part.
Replay moment two the same way. Notice what your body did naturally — your touch, your decision speed, your fearlessness.
Replay moment three. This time hold the feeling in your chest for ten seconds after it ends. That feeling is yours — you produced it.
Open your eyes. Say your power phrase once. This replay is your pre-match routine whenever confidence dips.
drills.journalPrompt: Which moment did you replay, and what did the best version of you do in it?

drills.title: Evidence Bank
drills.how: Log three pieces of proof after every session — confidence built on evidence doesn't collapse.
coachingPoints: Evidence survives bad games — hype doesn't
Small proof counts: one great touch is evidence
Read your bank before matches, not social media
steps: Understand the difference: hype confidence comes from feelings and compliments. Earned confidence comes from logged proof of work.
Think over your last session or match. Find three pieces of evidence: something you did well, something you improved, something you didn't quit on.
Be specific. Not 'played okay' — 'won four headers against a taller defender.'
Log them in the journal below. This is your evidence bank — entries add up across weeks.
Before your next match, read your last three entries instead of looking for reassurance anywhere else.
drills.journalPrompt: Write today's three pieces of evidence: one strength, one improvement, one moment you didn't quit.

drills.title: Weak-Foot Courage Block
drills.how: Ten minutes of weak-foot-only training to prove that discomfort is where ability grows.
coachingPoints: Ugly reps now buy clean reps later
Track progress weekly, not within one session
The lesson transfers: you can be bad at something and keep going
steps: Grab a ball and find a wall or open space. For the next ten minutes, your strong foot doesn't exist.
Block one (3 min): weak-foot passing against the wall. Count clean receptions out of every ten.
Block two (3 min): weak-foot dribbling in a small square — inside, outside, sole. Keep it slow and exact.
Block three (3 min): weak-foot finishing or driven passes at a target. Power comes last — accuracy first.
Final minute: notice what just happened. You did the uncomfortable thing for ten straight minutes. That's the muscle this exercise actually trains.
Log your wall-pass number — beat it next week.
drills.journalPrompt: What was your clean-reception count, and how did it feel to be a beginner again?

drills.title: Body Leads the Mind
drills.how: Use posture to drive confidence — the body convinces the brain, especially after mistakes.
coachingPoints: Opponents read body language — never show them a beaten player
Tall spine, eyes up, active feet
Posture first, feeling follows
steps: Stand up for this one. First, deliberately take a defeated posture: shoulders slumped, head down, slow feet. Hold ten seconds. Notice how your energy follows your shape.
Now switch: spine tall, chest open, chin level, feet bouncing lightly. Hold ten seconds. Feel the difference — same you, different signal.
Build your confident reset: after any mistake in a match, your body does three things in order — stand tall, eyes up to scan, feet moving.
Rehearse it: imagine missing a clear chance. Feel the urge to slump. Run the three-step posture reset instead.
Next match rule: whatever happens, the opposition never sees your head drop. Posture is a choice you control 100% of the time.
drills.journalPrompt: When does your body language betray you most, and what's your three-step reset?

drills.title: Demand the Ball
drills.how: Train the single biggest confidence behavior in soccer: wanting the ball when it matters.
coachingPoints: Hiding feels safe and costs you everything
Showing for the ball after a mistake is elite behavior
Judge yourself on involvement, not perfection
steps: Be honest: after a heavy touch or a giveaway, do you show for the next pass or drift away from play? Most players hide. They just don't call it that.
Set the standard: brave players are judged by touches wanted, not mistakes avoided.
Build your rule: within thirty seconds of any mistake, you must show for a pass, make a run, or demand the ball with your voice.
Rehearse it: picture giving the ball away and the opponent scoring from it. Now picture the restart — and you, hand up, calling for it. Feel how much courage that takes. That's the rep.
Track it next match: count the times you showed for the ball in the five minutes after each of your mistakes.
drills.journalPrompt: What's the moment in matches where you're most tempted to hide?

drills.title: Pre-Match Confidence Routine
drills.how: Assemble your tools into one repeatable 5-minute routine for every match day.
coachingPoints: Same routine every match — home, away, big, small
Routines beat moods
Five minutes, fully yours, phone away
steps: You now have the pieces: highlight replay, evidence bank, power phrase, box breathing, first-five script. This exercise locks them into one routine.
Minute 1–2: box breathing, six slow cycles. Get the body quiet.
Minute 3: highlight replay — one best moment, full detail, through your own eyes.
Minute 4: read (or recall) your last three evidence bank entries. Proof, not hype.
Minute 5: say your power phrase, then run your first-five script — your first three simple actions of the match.
Walk through the whole five minutes now as a rehearsal. Use it before every match from here on.
drills.journalPrompt: Write your five-minute routine in your own words — what happens in each minute?

categories.name: Composure
categories.focus: Stay calm and clear when the game heats up.

drills.title: Long Exhale Reset
drills.how: A fast-acting breath — short in, long out — that lowers the body's alarm in seconds.
coachingPoints: The long exhale is the off-switch
Usable mid-match in under ten seconds
Two breaths are enough at a penalty or free kick
steps: This breath works faster than box breathing: in through the nose for 4 seconds, out slowly through the mouth for 8.
Complete 5 cycles with the animation. Let the exhale empty completely before breathing in again.
Feel the drop — heart rate, shoulders, jaw. The long exhale tells your nervous system the danger has passed.
Map your match moments: before a penalty, after conceding, when the crowd or sideline gets loud. Two of these breaths fit anywhere a dead ball gives you ten seconds.
drills.journalPrompt: What match situation spikes your nerves the most?

drills.title: Pressure Rehearsal
drills.how: Visualize high-pressure moments in advance so match pressure feels familiar, not new.
coachingPoints: Rehearse the FEELING of pressure, then the response
Always end the scene with a good action
Familiar pressure is half pressure
steps: Close your eyes between steps. Scene one: last minute, draw, your team wins a penalty — and you're taking it. Feel the real nerves: legs, stomach, noise.
Inside the scene, run your tools: long exhale twice, pick your corner, power phrase. Strike it clean. Watch it hit the net. Hold that for five seconds.
Scene two: you've just conceded, ninetieth minute is approaching, the opposition is celebrating. Feel the frustration. Now: posture reset, reset word, organize your team for the restart.
Scene three: build your own — the situation that rattles YOU most. Feel it fully, then respond with your tools and end the scene on your terms.
Open your eyes. You've now been in those moments. When they arrive for real, they'll feel like a place you've already played.
drills.journalPrompt: Which pressure scene felt most real, and which tool worked in it?

drills.title: Frustration Rules
drills.how: Write your personal rules for the three moments most likely to make you lose your head.
coachingPoints: Decide your response BEFORE the moment, not during
A rule removes the decision when emotions are high
Referees, opponents, and scorelines test everyone — rules are the difference
steps: Identify your three triggers — the moments that genuinely heat you up. Common ones: a bad referee call, an opponent's fouling or talking, a teammate's mistake, being subbed off, going behind.
For each trigger, write one rule. A rule is an if-then: 'IF the referee misses a foul on me, THEN one long exhale, posture tall, and I'm sprinting into position before I finish the breath.'
Keep each rule physical and immediate — something your body does, not something you try to feel.
Rehearse each rule once: feel the trigger, run the rule.
Log your three rules below. Re-read them before any match you expect to be heated.
drills.journalPrompt: Write your three if-then frustration rules.

levels.name: Match Application
levels.theme: Slow the game down when it speeds up.

drills.title: Slow Is Smooth
drills.how: Train the composed player's secret: when everything speeds up, your touch slows down.
coachingPoints: Rushing is fear wearing a work-rate costume
One extra touch of control beats a fast giveaway
Calm is contagious — one composed player settles a team
steps: The idea: under pressure, most players speed everything up — touch, decisions, breathing — and accuracy collapses. Composed players do the opposite at the right moments.

With a ball, rehearse it physically: play a firm pass against a wall, and as the ball returns imagine a defender closing fast. Take ONE controlled touch out of their line before you play on. Repeat ten times.
Now rehearse the decision version: ball arrives, you're surrounded — is the right play the brave dribble or the simple one-touch pass to safety? Composure means choosing on purpose, not in panic.
Add the breath: in matches, your cue is the long exhale as the ball travels to you. Exhale, touch, decide.
Next match: find three moments to deliberately slow your touch when the game is frantic. Count them.
drills.journalPrompt: Where in matches do you rush most — touch, passes, or decisions?

drills.title: The 24-Hour Rule
drills.how: A structured way to process a bad game — feel it, learn from it, close it within 24 hours.
coachingPoints: You're allowed to be disappointed — briefly and on purpose
Extract lessons, not punishment
After 24 hours the game is closed — next action
steps: Use this after a bad match or session. Step one: allow the disappointment. Ten honest minutes — don't fake positivity, don't replay it for three days either.
Step two: extract exactly two lessons. One technical or tactical ('I got beaten on my back shoulder twice — track the runner earlier'), one mental ('My head dropped after the first mistake').
Step three: turn each lesson into one action for the coming week — a drill to run, a rule to apply, an intention for the next session.
Step four: find one thing that was genuinely good. There is always one. Add it to your evidence bank.
Step five: say your reset word. The game is now closed. Re-opening it is against the rule.
drills.journalPrompt: Two lessons from your last bad game, and the one action each lesson becomes.

drills.title: Captain of the Storm
drills.how: Learn to be the calmest player on the pitch when the match turns chaotic.
coachingPoints: Teams mirror their calmest loud player
Instructions calm people — panic spreads faster than calm
Your composure is also FOR your teammates
steps: Close your eyes between steps. The scene: your team is 1–0 up with ten minutes left. The opposition throws everything forward. Your teammates are panicking — hoofing clearances, arguing, chasing wildly.
See yourself as the calm one. Long exhale. Tall posture. You start talking: 'Compact. Stay with your runner. Time on the ball — look first.'
The ball comes to you under heavy pressure. Slow is smooth: controlled touch, simple pass, no drama. Feel how your calm play and clear voice settle the players around you.
Run the scene once more, but losing 1–0 instead: same calm, same voice, now driving urgency WITHOUT panic — 'Quick restart. Quality ball in. Believe.'
Open your eyes. In your next match, take one chaotic stretch and deliberately be its calmest voice.
drills.journalPrompt: Who is the calmest player you've ever played with or watched — what exactly do they do?

categories.name: Match Mentality
categories.focus: Standards, discipline, and the habits that compound.

levels.name: Foundation
levels.theme: Set standards. Keep them when nobody's watching.

drills.title: Non-Negotiables
drills.how: Define the three standards you bring to every single session, regardless of mood.
coachingPoints: Standards are behaviors, not outcomes
Three is enough — keep them keepable
Motivation follows action, not the other way round
steps: The difference between players who make it and players who don't is rarely talent. It's standards held on ordinary days.

Choose three non-negotiables — behaviors you bring to EVERY session, tired or fresh, motivated or flat. Examples: 'First one moving in the warm-up.' 'Sprint every recovery run.' 'No phone until training is done.'
Test each one: would you keep it on your worst day? If not, shrink it until you would.
Write them below. They're now your floor — your performance can vary, your standards can't.
Review weekly: which did you keep all week, which slipped, and does one need to change?
drills.journalPrompt: Write your three non-negotiables.

drills.title: Do It Anyway
drills.how: Train on a low-motivation day on purpose — and learn what actually gets you moving.
coachingPoints: Start before you feel ready — readiness follows starting
Shrink the start, not the session
Discipline is a skill with reps, like passing
steps: This exercise is for a day you don't feel like training. If today is that day, perfect. If not, save it and come back.
Learn the five-minute contract: you only owe five minutes. Anyone can do five minutes. Quitting after five is allowed — but you must start.
Shrink the start: boots on, ball out, one simple drill. No warm-up speeches. The first touch is the hardest rep of the day.
Do your five minutes now or at your next opportunity. Notice what happens around minute four — almost everyone keeps going.
Whatever you did, log it. A ten-minute session on a zero-motivation day is worth more to your career than an hour on a perfect one.
drills.journalPrompt: What did you tell yourself today to start — and did you stop at five minutes?

drills.title: The Extra Rep
drills.how: End every session with one extra block after the moment you wanted to stop.
coachingPoints: The session truly starts when you want it to end
Choose the extra in advance — decisions made tired are skipped
Small daily extras compound into visible separation
steps: The idea: every player trains until tired. The separation happens in what you do AFTER tired arrives.
Define your extra rep menu now — three small finishers you can attach to any session: e.g. 10 weak-foot finishes, 20 sharp toe taps at max speed, 5 full-pitch-tempo sprints.
The rule: when a session ends and you feel done, you pick ONE item off your menu before you walk off.
Why pre-deciding matters: tired brains don't make brave choices. The menu makes it automatic.
Apply it for one week, every session. Then look at your training log and count seven extras nobody asked you for.
drills.journalPrompt: What three finishers are on your extra-rep menu?

levels.name: Match Application
levels.theme: Goals, reflection, and the long game.

drills.title: Goal Ladder
drills.how: Build a three-rung ladder: season goal, monthly target, weekly action — each rung reachable from the one below.
coachingPoints: Dream goals need working rungs underneath
Weekly actions must be fully in your control
Review the ladder monthly — adjust rungs, keep climbing
steps: Top rung — season goal: where do you want to be when this season ends? Make it concrete: starting spot, position, a number (goals, assists, clean sheets), a team you want to make.
Middle rung — this month: what measurable improvement this month makes the season goal more likely? E.g. 'weak foot trustworthy in matches', 'win 60% of my duels', 'first-choice at left back'.
Bottom rung — this week: what actions, fully in your control, serve the monthly target? E.g. 'four sessions, two with weak-foot blocks', 'extra rep after every session'.
Check the ladder: does each rung actually lead to the one above? If a rung depends on luck or a coach's opinion, rewrite it as an action you control.
Write all three rungs below. Re-read the bottom rung before every session this week.
drills.journalPrompt: Write your ladder: season goal, monthly target, this week's actions.

drills.title: Sunday Review
drills.how: A weekly ten-minute review: what worked, what didn't, what changes next week.
coachingPoints: Reviewed weeks compound — unreviewed weeks repeat
Be a fair coach to yourself: honest AND constructive
End every review with next week's single focus
steps: Do this once a week, same day, ten minutes. Look at your training log for the week first.
Question one — volume: how many sessions, and did you keep your non-negotiables in each?
Question two — quality: what genuinely improved this week? Name the evidence.
Question three — honesty: what did you avoid, skip, or coast through? No drama, just the fact.
Question four — direction: based on the above, what is NEXT week's single focus, and does your goal ladder need a rung adjusted?
Log your answers below. Twenty of these reviews is a transformed player.
drills.journalPrompt: This week: sessions completed, what improved, what you avoided, next week's focus.

drills.title: Play Your Game
drills.how: Define your game in three sentences — and commit to playing it regardless of occasion or opponent.
coachingPoints: Big matches are won by players who stay themselves
Your identity travels to every pitch — occasions don't change it
Three sentences, known by heart
steps: The trap: in trials, finals, and big matches, players abandon their game — the dribbler stops dribbling, the talker goes quiet, the presser hesitates. Pressure makes players generic.

Define your game in three sentences. Sentence one: your superpower ('I take defenders on in the final third'). Sentence two: your engine ('I press first and recover fastest'). Sentence three: your presence ('I talk constantly and lift heads').
Test them: would your teammates recognize you from these three sentences? If not, rewrite until they would.
Commit: these three sentences play EVERY match. The bigger the occasion, the more deliberately you play them. Scouts and coaches pick distinct players, not safe ones.
Memorize them now — say all three twice. Add them to the end of your pre-match routine, right after your power phrase.
drills.journalPrompt: Write the three sentences that define your game.
